---
title: "Describing Data: risks guide"
subtitle: "MC 451 and MC 501 · the traps on worksheet 2 of the Twitch job"
---

This guide goes with the Describing Data worksheet
([MC 451](../../starters/12-describing-data-mc451.qmd), [MC 501](../../starters/12-describing-data-mc501.qmd)).
It does not fill in the worksheet. Each section names a trap, shows what it looks like on the
Twitch data, and gives you a check. Every output below is real.

Words such as median, skew, outlier, and cross-tabulation are defined in plain English in the
worksheet's **Key terms** table.

## 1. A table that is mostly `NA`

**What it looks like.** Only your thirty messages carry a code, so counting the hand-coded
variable across the whole table puts almost everything in an `NA` row:

```
  reaction_only     n
1 commentary       17
2 reaction         13
3 <NA>          35237
```

A summary of the whole table has the same problem in a different form: `mean()` of a column with
any missing value returns `NA`.

**How to check.** Before you describe a variable, ask which rows have it. For your code, the
groups in any table or summary must add to 30. For a mean, median, or standard deviation, report
the `n` it was computed on.

## 2. A mean that hides the shape

**What it looks like.** Message length has a mean of 29.0 characters and a median of 17. A few
very long messages (the longest is 501 characters) pull the mean far above the typical message.
Reported alone, the mean describes a message almost nobody sent.

**How to check.** Report the mean, the median, and the standard deviation together. When the
mean and median disagree, say so in a sentence and say what it means about the distribution.

## 3. Counts that measure the sampling, not the platform

**What it looks like.** The corpus took up to 1,000 messages from each of fifty channels. So
Fortnite and League of Legends each have exactly 4,000 messages: four channels each, not four
thousand people choosing them. Hearthstone has 3,004 messages from eleven channels.

**How to check.** Next to any count of messages by category, count the channels behind it with
`n_distinct(channel)`. Then write the interpretation about this corpus, not about Twitch.

## 4. A variable that belongs to the channel

**What it looks like.** `viewer_band` and `channel_type` are one value per channel, copied onto
every message. The large band holds 2,000 messages, but only two channels:

```
  viewer_band     n
1 small          41
2 medium          7
3 large           2
```

That is a count of channels per band, and it is the number that limits what the band can show.

**How to check.** Count distinct channels per category (`distinct(channel, viewer_band)`, then
`count()`), and say how many channels stand behind any comparison you describe.

## 5. An empty cell that reads as missing

**What it looks like.** No large-band channel is non-gaming, so that combination never occurs.
`pivot_wider()` has nothing to put there and writes `NA`:

```
  viewer_band gaming `non-gaming`
3 large         2000           NA
```

A reader takes `NA` to mean "unknown". Here the true count is zero.

**How to check.** Read every `NA` in a cross-tabulation and ask whether the value is unknown or
is zero. A combination that never occurs is a zero, and the table should say so.

## 6. A chart that drops rows without saying

**What it looks like.** Capping the x axis at 200 characters removes the messages beyond it.
ggplot2 mentions it once, as a warning that is easy to miss:

```
Removed 365 rows containing non-finite outside the scale range (`stat_bin()`).
```

That is 361 long messages plus the 4 with no text. The chart looks complete.

**How to check.** Read every warning a chart prints. Then count what you left out and disclose
it, in the caption and in your disclosure sentence.

## 7. Proportions that hide sizes

**What it looks like.** A bar chart with `position = "fill"` makes every bar the same height, so
the small band (27,766 messages) and the large band (2,000) look equally weighty.

**How to check.** If a chart shows shares, give the counts somewhere a reader will see them: the
caption, the table beside it, or your interpretation.

## 8. Every point drawn twice

**What it looks like.** A boxplot draws its outliers as dots. Adding `geom_jitter()` to show every
message draws those same messages a second time, so the longest message appears as two dots side
by side.

**How to check.** Count the dots above the box against the number of outliers you expect. When
you add your own points, turn the boxplot's off.

## 9. Alt text that repeats the title

**What it looks like.** Alt text that says "Bar chart of channel type by viewer band" tells a
reader who cannot see the chart only what the title already said, and nothing about what the
chart shows.

**How to check.** Read your alt text without looking at the chart. Does it say what pattern a
sighted reader would see, such as which group is larger and by roughly how much? If not, it is a
label, not a description.

## 10. A figure saved by hand

**What it looks like.** A chart exported with a button or a screenshot exists once. Change one
line and the file in `figures/` no longer matches the code.

**How to check.** Delete the `figures` folder and render the worksheet. Every chart should come
back.

## 11. Bars in an order that means nothing

**What it looks like.** Categories plot in alphabetical order unless you set another one, so a
bar chart of games runs from A to Z instead of from most to least.

**How to check.** Look at the order of the bars and ask whether it carries information. If not,
order them by size or by their natural order.

## MC 501: diagnostics shown, not asserted

**What it looks like.** "The data look roughly normal" is an assertion. Message length is
strongly right-skewed in every viewer band, and the spread differs a great deal across bands (a
standard deviation of 53.9 characters in the medium band against 31.1 in the large one), so a
sentence like that would be wrong as well as unsupported.

**How to check.** For each claim about shape, spread, an assumption, or an outlier, point to the
output that shows it: the histogram, the group standard deviations, the expected counts, or the
values `boxplot.stats()` lists.
